title: The Investing Fascia–Carotid Sheath–Vagus Nerve Mechanical Coupling Hypothesis: PIEZO Mechanotransduction and Directions for Validation
content: The vagus nerve travels through the carotid sheath in the neck. Its functional status has long been regarded as independent of the surrounding fascial environment. This article proposes the “Investing Fascia–Carotid Sheath–Vagus Nerve Mechanical Coupling Hypothesis.” Its central premise is that fibrotic thickening of the investing fascia—the superficial layer of the deep cervical fascia in the posterior triangle and between the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles—or of the deep cervical fascial layers in the anterior triangle may transmit abnormal mechanical loads through the deep cervical fascial network to the carotid sheath. This transmission may alter the intra-sheath microenvironment and modulate vagal afferent and efferent activity. The result would be a mechanical coupling pathway linking tension in the superficial deep cervical fascia and deep cervical fascial network to the intra-sheath mechanical microenvironment and vagal tone. Recent anatomical, imaging, molecular, and clinical intervention studies suggest that the three layers of the deep cervical fascia—the investing fascia, the pretracheal fascia, and the prevertebral fascia—may form a structural coupling with the carotid sheath through a continuous or semi-continuous mechanical network. Together, these layers may constitute a fascial–sheath mechanical continuum capable of transmitting mechanical signals from the neck to the vagus nerve. PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 are core molecular components of vagal mechanotransduction. Their expression and function are regulated at multiple levels by MDFIC2, Nedd4-2, GPR146, ZBED6, and the neuroimmune microenvironment. Mechanosensitive potassium channels, TRPV2, TRPM4, and other channels participate cooperatively, suggesting that PIEZO channels are necessary but not necessarily the only molecular components. The cross-sectional area (CSA) of the cervical vagus nerve is reduced in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS). In contrast, CSA may be increased in metabolic diseases such as diabetic neuropathy. These findings suggest that the direction of CSA change may be disease-specific. This article systematically reviews the anatomical basis, mechanical transmission pathways, molecular conversion mechanisms, functional validation evidence, and clinical implications of this hypothesis and proposes testable directions for validation. Critically, the middle segment of this hypothetical chain—fascial mechanical changes, carotid sheath deformation, changes in the intra-sheath microenvironment, and changes in vagal mechanical exposure—currently lacks synchronized in vivo measurements in the same participant. This segment should be labeled as theoretical inference or pending direct validation, not as an established mechanism.
